A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with MJGD/MJSD renamed MTJD/MTAD. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original decoding benchmarks, energy measurements, and beam-count and acceptance-threshold experiments in Sections 3–5.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds downstream evaluations, larger-model results, and sampling and fine-tuning analyses, including Appendix C.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 is identical after normalizing the method name. Both versions use auxiliary-model beam drafting, joint-likelihood verification, longest-prefix acceptance, and an additional target-model token. v1 already documents stochastic top-k/top-p sampling; v2's terminology and expanded explanation do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: v2 retains ChatGPT-Prompt, ChatAlpaca, and CNN/DailyMail and adds Spider text-to-SQL and MT-Bench evaluation. These introduce substantive task coverage, including structured query generation and math, coding, reasoning, and other conversational tasks.

E2.justification: SpecInfer, unsuccessful because of memory limits in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator in v2 Tables 4 and 9. The main benchmark table drops the greedy comparator, although it remains in other comparisons. The block-efficiency comparison also expands from speculative decoding versus the proposed method to all five methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds OPT-30B and Llama-2-Chat-70B configurations, downstream scoring, fine-tuning controls, and a GPT-3.5 experiment selecting among ten outputs generated at temperature 2. Block efficiency measures generated tokens rather than just accepted draft tokens. Section 4 also changes the reported batch-study hardware from two 24GB A10 GPUs to one 48GB L40 while retaining identical results; this establishes a reporting change, not a confirmed rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a perplexity-versus-execution-accuracy analysis, top-k/top-p sensitivity tests, and comparisons of no fine-tuning, draft-only fine-tuning, and fine-tuning both models (Table 1 and Appendix C.2–C.3). The original beam-count and acceptance-threshold analyses remain, while block-efficiency analysis expands.

E5.justification: Both versions report four experimental repetitions and standard deviations. v2 additionally states that MT-Bench deviations include variation across tasks, and Table 9 reports means and deviations across datasets. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark entries in v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 4 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparator, benchmark, larger-model, and downstream results. Table 6 newly reports MTAD/speculative Spider accuracy of 13.0/11.5 and MT-Bench averages of 2.68/2.58, with several category declines. Expanded-coverage speed and energy ratios become 1.42×/1.54× versus 1.49×/1.62×; these are aggregate changes. Section 5.1 also changes the comparator for the claimed 21.2% perplexity reduction from BiLD to speculative decoding.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix F offers a heuristic score-function argument. v2 replaces it with asymptotic perplexity analysis, a greedy-decoding comparison, approximation-error and acceptance-length bounds, and proofs in Appendix A (Theorem 3.2 through Theorem 3.6). The energy decomposition remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction move from empirical and heuristic support for joint decoding to explicit claims of theoretical perplexity improvement and bounded approximation error. They also broaden the stated empirical contribution to downstream effectiveness and models up to 70B parameters, while retaining the central quality-and-efficiency objective.

C2.justification: v2 interprets its new bounds as convergence toward exact joint decoding and discusses limited gains and memory costs from multiple-draft extensions. It adds verification-overhead explanations for SpecInfer/Spectr performance. v1's explicit warning that improved perplexity may not improve downstream effectiveness is removed with Section 8, although a shorter well-trained-model qualification remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies hyperparameters for SpecInfer and the added datasets and revises the batch-study hardware description. However, its dataset-statistics table removes the test-input-count column. Existing code access, power-measurement instructions, and most configuration details are retained; the new fine-tuning experiments lack detailed training recipes.

R1.justification: v2 adds EAGLE/MEDUSA positioning as complementary drafting approaches, citations for decoding evaluation, Spider, and MT-Bench, and removes the de Vries energy-footprint reference. The broader positioning against speculative and non-autoregressive decoding remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten, including an explicit contribution list. Sampling terminology and the preliminaries are revised throughout. The appendices are reorganized around proofs and additional experiments, and the limitations-and-impact section is removed.

P2.justification: The main benchmark table is restructured with added datasets and SpecInfer, removing greedy and speed-up rows. The per-dataset acceptance bar chart is replaced by an aggregate block-efficiency table. v2 adds multiple downstream and appendix tables, expands the hyperparameter table, and relocates the retained threshold plot; Figures 1 and 2 remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support through downstream metrics, SpecInfer comparisons, larger models, and fine-tuning controls. However, its central new guarantees have unresolved reasoning gaps: Appendix A.2 compares fixed prefixes without addressing the differing histories acknowledged in v1 Appendix F, and Theorem 3.6 omits the algorithm's finite draft-length cap. Removing the explicit downstream-performance limitation and test-count reporting also reduces transparency. The empirical gains and concerns about the stronger theoretical claims prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
